items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.original_title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.rss_title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.rss_description: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges Claims ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:52 Hurricane Isaias shows how quickly claims surge after quiet periods, straining leaner teams to review complex restoration invoices thoroughly. October 29, 2026 Image Hurricane Isaias spun up in the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, just two days after becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, the latest first hurricane in more than a century. Its sudden arrival is a reminder of how quickly a quiet claims environment can change. For property claims teams, the workload extends well beyond the initial wave of reported losses. Damage to hotels, apartment communities, retail centers and industrial properties can lead to large restoration projects and complex invoices that arrive over the weeks and months that follow. Early modeled estimates of privately insured losses range from $1 billion to $2 billion (Verisk) to $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (Moody's RMS). While AM Best expects it to be an earnings event for insurers rather than a capital event, the storm created a substantial uptick in work for claims and restoration teams. The aerial imagery firm Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including more than 3,100 with major damage. A high-rise condominium resort on Pensacola Beach lost windows across two towers, and an apartment complex in Milton, Fla., lost much of its roof. Damage like that becomes restoration projects, and restoration projects become invoices. Isaias follows a prolonged stretch of slower claims activity. Industry data puts commercial property claims at 710,000 in 2025, down from 910,000 in 2023. A separate measure, U.S. property claim assignments , fell 12% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and ran 13% below the five-year average, extending a four-year decline. These are different Verisk datasets, but both point to a slower claims environment. More of the work that remains also arrives in bursts: catastrophe claims made up 43% of second-quarter volume, up from 34% five years earlier. No claims organization can staff indefinitely for a catastrophe-level workload during a stretch like this. Nor should it. Teams that have adjusted staffing and resources to match lower demand face a particular challenge: claims volume can rebound much faster than review capacity can be rebuilt. When restoration invoices pile up, those leaner teams face a difficult trade-off. Bills can wait for a thorough audit, extending claim cycle times, or move through with less scrutiny, increasing the risk of leakage. Automation offers a way to absorb more work without having to rebuild the entire manual review operation. The surge also has a long tail. When Hurricane Sally struck the same stretch of coast in 2020, Florida insurers had closed about two-thirds of residential claims six weeks later, but only 13% of commercial property claims. Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida on Sept. 28, 2022. In the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's March 4, 2025, snapshot , 96% of the 789,066 reported Ian claims were closed. Yet 6,628 of the 32,850 commercial property claims remained open nearly two and a half years after the storm. Those figures do not establish whether the delays involved coverage, reconstruction, invoice review, or disputes. They do show how long commercial claims work can continue after the initial surge. The bottleneck moves as the claim progresses An initial wave of assignments is only the beginning. Adjusters must address coverage, communicate with insureds, inspect damage, review scopes and estimates, and coordinate recovery. Restoration invoices arrive as work progresses, often while those adjusters are still managing both new and existing claims. Large restoration projects can involve multiple crews, weeks of drying equipment, substantial material charges, and several subcontractors. The resulting invoices can be complex even under normal conditions. When many arrive together, claims teams face two pressures at once: more invoices to review and more work required to review each one thoroughly. An invoice is not simply a total to approve. Time-and-materials bills can require checking labor hours and classifications, equipment usage and duration, agreed rates, materials, subcontractor charges, markups, and arithmetic. A reviewer may need to compare the invoice with supporting records and the work performed. That takes time, and the work does not become less necessary because the team has fewer people available. Both delayed reviews and unsupported payments carry consequences for the insured, the carrier, and the restoration contractor waiting to be paid. Adding more reviewers can help, but it takes time to find, train, and coordinate them. It also raises the cost of handling a temporary spike. The more useful question is which repeatable parts of review can be completed consistently without requiring a few more hours of specialist time for every additional invoice. How automation can absorb a surge AI-enhanced automation can help teams review restoration invoices faster by extracting and sorting line items and running calculations to identify charges that need a closer look. During a surge, these capabilities support consistent, thorough review. AI can help turn invoice documents into organized data, while programmed audit rules check calculations and compare charges with agreed rates or benchmarks. The adjuster or specialist still has to consider the work performed, evaluate the findings, and resolve disagreements. Automation reduces the manual checking that precedes those decisions. Rest-Assured has pioneered the use of AI-enhanced automation in restoration invoice auditing. Property insurers have used the platform to audit nearly $1 billion in property restoration invoices, uncovering documented findings to guide claims professionals through review and resolution. Measure the effect on the claim The right measure is not merely how fast an audit comes back. Claims leaders should look at the time from invoice receipt to a documented review, how long exceptions take to resolve, the rate of confirmed findings, the cost per review, and whether payment disagreements are cleared sooner. Those measures show whether faster processing is actually helping the claim move toward resolution. What to put in place before the invoices arrive Mitigation invoices begin arriving within weeks of landfall, and larger reconstruction bills follow for months. That gap is the time to prepare. Some insurers are already using automation to take on the time-intensive parts of invoice review, putting them in a better position to handle the next surge. A few decisions made now can keep review from becoming the bottleneck later: Confirm the rate agreements, pricing guidelines, and benchmarks reviewers will apply, including how post-storm pricing will be evaluated. Set one intake path for restoration invoices and define the supporting documentation each one needs. Identify which repeatable review steps, such as line-item extraction, arithmetic and rate checks, can be automated. Decide which findings can be resolved routinely and which require an adjuster or specialist. Decide in advance where overflow review goes if volume exceeds internal capacity. Claims teams cannot maintain catastrophe-level staffing through every quiet period. They need a review process that can expand when demand returns. Automating time-intensive invoice checks can help leaner teams absorb a surge without forcing a choice between longer cycle times and greater leakage. Restoration invoice auditing does not have to be a bottleneck, and keeping claims moving does not have to mean letting invoices pass through without scrutiny. items.extracted_text: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges | Insurance Thought Leadership Skip to main content Claims Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges Hurricane Isaias shows how quickly claims surge after quiet periods, straining leaner teams to review complex restoration invoices thoroughly. Jeff Esper October 29, 2026 Hurricane Isaias spun up in the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, just two days after becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, the latest first hurricane in more than a century. Its sudden arrival is a reminder of how quickly a quiet claims environment can change. For property claims teams, the workload extends well beyond the initial wave of reported losses. Damage to hotels, apartment communities, retail centers and industrial properties can lead to large restoration projects and complex invoices that arrive over the weeks and months that follow. Early modeled estimates of privately insured losses range from $1 billion to $2 billion (Verisk) to $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (Moody's RMS). While AM Best expects it to be an earnings event for insurers rather than a capital event, the storm created a substantial uptick in work for claims and restoration teams. The aerial imagery firm Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including more than 3,100 with major damage. A high-rise condominium resort on Pensacola Beach lost windows across two towers, and an apartment complex in Milton, Fla., lost much of its roof. Damage like that becomes restoration projects, and restoration projects become invoices. Isaias follows a prolonged stretch of slower claims activity. Industry data puts commercial property claims at 710,000 in 2025, down from 910,000 in 2023. A separate measure, U.S. property claim assignments , fell 12% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and ran 13% below the five-year average, extending a four-year decline. These are different Verisk datasets, but both point to a slower claims environment. More of the work that remains also arrives in bursts: catastrophe claims made up 43% of second-quarter volume, up from 34% five years earlier. No claims organization can staff indefinitely for a catastrophe-level workload during a stretch like this. Nor should it. Teams that have adjusted staffing and resources to match lower demand face a particular challenge: claims volume can rebound much faster than review capacity can be rebuilt. When restoration invoices pile up, those leaner teams face a difficult trade-off. Bills can wait for a thorough audit, extending claim cycle times, or move through with less scrutiny, increasing the risk of leakage. Automation offers a way to absorb more work without having to rebuild the entire manual review operation. The surge also has a long tail. When Hurricane Sally struck the same stretch of coast in 2020, Florida insurers had closed about two-thirds of residential claims six weeks later, but only 13% of commercial property claims. Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida on Sept. 28, 2022. In the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's March 4, 2025, snapshot , 96% of the 789,066 reported Ian claims were closed. Yet 6,628 of the 32,850 commercial property claims remained open nearly two and a half years after the storm. Those figures do not establish whether the delays involved coverage, reconstruction, invoice review, or disputes. They do show how long commercial claims work can continue after the initial surge. The bottleneck moves as the claim progresses An initial wave of assignments is only the beginning. Adjusters must address coverage, communicate with insureds, inspect damage, review scopes and estimates, and coordinate recovery. Restoration invoices arrive as work progresses, often while those adjusters are still managing both new and existing claims. Large restoration projects can involve multiple crews, weeks of drying equipment, substantial material charges, and several subcontractors. The resulting invoices can be complex even under normal conditions. When many arrive together, claims teams face two pressures at once: more invoices to review and more work required to review each one thoroughly. An invoice is not simply a total to approve. Time-and-materials bills can require checking labor hours and classifications, equipment usage and duration, agreed rates, materials, subcontractor charges, markups, and arithmetic. A reviewer may need to compare the invoice with supporting records and the work performed. That takes time, and the work does not become less necessary because the team has fewer people available. Both delayed reviews and unsupported payments carry consequences for the insured, the carrier, and the restoration contractor waiting to be paid. Adding more reviewers can help, but it takes time to find, train, and coordinate them. It also raises the cost of handling a temporary spike. The more useful question is which repeatable parts of review can be completed consistently without requiring a few more hours of specialist time for every additional invoice. How automation can absorb a surge AI-enhanced automation can help teams review restoration invoices faster by extracting and sorting line items and running calculations to identify charges that need a closer look. During a surge, these capabilities support consistent, thorough review. AI can help turn invoice documents into organized data, while programmed audit rules check calculations and compare charges with agreed rates or benchmarks. The adjuster or specialist still has to consider the work performed, evaluate the findings, and resolve disagreements. Automation reduces the manual checking that precedes those decisions. Rest-Assured has pioneered the use of AI-enhanced automation in restoration invoice auditing. Property insurers have used the platform to audit nearly $1 billion in property restoration invoices, uncovering documented findings to guide claims professionals through review and resolution. Measure the effect on the claim The right measure is not merely how fast an audit comes back. Claims leaders should look at the time from invoice receipt to a documented review, how long exceptions take to resolve, the rate of confirmed findings, the cost per review, and whether payment disagreements are cleared sooner. Those measures show whether faster processing is actually helping the claim move toward resolution. What to put in place before the invoices arrive Mitigation invoices begin arriving within weeks of landfall, and larger reconstruction bills follow for months. That gap is the time to prepare. Some insurers are already using automation to take on the time-intensive parts of invoice review, putting them in a better position to handle the next surge. A few decisions made now can keep review from becoming the bottleneck later: Confirm the rate agreements, pricing guidelines, and benchmarks reviewers will apply, including how post-storm pricing will be evaluated. Set one intake path for restoration invoices and define the supporting documentation each one needs. Identify which repeatable review steps, such as line-item extraction, arithmetic and rate checks, can be automated. Decide which findings can be resolved routinely and which require an adjuster or specialist. Decide in advance where overflow review goes if volume exceeds internal capacity. Claims teams cannot maintain catastrophe-level staffing through every quiet period. They need a review process that can expand when demand returns. Automating time-intensive invoice checks can help leaner teams absorb a surge without forcing a choice between longer cycle times and greater leakage. Restoration invoice auditing does not have to be a bottleneck, and keeping claims moving does not have to mean letting invoices pass through without scrutiny. items.title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?

items.rss_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.original_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

According to Jordan Nickerson, Co-founder at Icosa Investments AG, navigating the year-end renewals successfully will depend on how effectively ILS managers balance pricing adjustments with contract terms and liquidity. Speaking to Artemis recently, Nickerson outlined how discipline and consistency in the ILS market is just as much a question of instrument format as it is of investment expertise. In terms of what topics specialist catastrophe bond manager Icosa Investments foresees ILS markets and alternative capital managers taking into their year-end renewal negotiations, Nickerson highlighted ILS yields as a key area of interest. “In our view, the central theme is normalisation. Yields in insurance-linked securities (ILS) remain above their historical average, supported by higher collateral returns, but transaction multiples now sit closer to long-term norms than to the post-Ian highs,” Nickerson explained to Artemis. Another crucial topic that Icosa expects to feature heavily during year-end renewal negotiations is cycle preparedness. “Softening tends to be gradual hardening typically happens quickly. When it is driven by catastrophe events, it can coincide with trapped collateral, making sudden rate increases hard to capture. That puts a premium on flexibility and liquidity within an ILS allocation,” Nickerson noted. He continued: “Hence, we believe discipline and consistency in ILS is at least as much a question of instrument format as it is of investment expertise.” Turning attention to investor sentiment, Nickerson expects allocators to remain constructive ahead of year-end, albeit increasingly selective. The executive outlined that Icosa expects liquidity, risk concentration, transparency, and expected return robustness to take precedence over pure deployment volume. Moreover, to navigate these shifting investor priorities, Nickerson noted that Icosa draws a clear distinction between what he calls Foundational ILS and Evolving ILS. “Foundational ILS covers cat bonds and private property catastrophe strategies: predominantly low frequency, event-driven, short-tail risk with limited financial-market correlation, the characteristics around which the asset class originally developed. Evolving ILS covers the newer extensions of the market, most prominently cyber and casualty,” Nickerson said. He continued: “Within Evolving ILS, cyber is a relatively natural extension given its event-driven character, though its behaviour in a truly systemic event remains untested. Casualty ILS is a more distinct proposition: higher-frequency, longer-tail risk in which part of the ultimate return may depend on how capital is invested during the risk period, potentially reducing the diversification benefit that sits at the heart of Foundational ILS. “We expect appetite to become increasingly differentiated across these segments.” While industry sentiment indicates that discipline will hold on key contract features at the upcoming January renewals, Nickerson emphasised that he expects the renewal period to still be competitive, particularly if catastrophe activity stays light through the second half of 2026. “We expect the next renewals to remain competitive, particularly if catastrophe activity stays light through the second half, though not at the pricing pace of the past twelve months, with differentiation by risk quality becoming more important,” Nickerson said. “The key distinction, in our view, is between price movement and changes in the quality of risk transfer. A lower spread – with other terms and conditions unchanged – can be assessed transparently on a risk adjusted basis a lower attachment, broader coverage or looser wording changes the nature of the risk itself. Price and structure are not, in our view, interchangeable concessions. Concluding: “Ultimately, discipline does not mean every term stays unchanged. It means understanding exactly what is being conceded, why, and whether the compensation remains appropriate for the resulting risk.” Read all of our interviews with ILS market and reinsurance sector professionals here . items.title: AI presents risks, opportunities for women
items.original_title: AI presents risks, opportunities for women
items.rss_title: AI presents risks, opportunities for women
items.rss_description: Artificial intelligence could pose particular challenges for women in insurance because they hold many of the administrative roles susceptible to automation, but the technology also presents opportunities, industry experts say.
items.extracted_text: Insurers should focus on improving work rather than cutting jobs, while employees need to develop AI skills, speakers said during presentations at the Business Insurance Women to Watch Leadership Conference Thursday. Women perform a disproportionate share of administrative work in claims and underwriting, where AI can increasingly handle repetitive tasks, said Michelle Raue, Nashville-based founder of Raue Strategic Advisory. Automating those tasks could free employees to spend more time with policyholders, particularly during the claims process, she said. “People have a loss, and they want to tell a human about their loss,” Ms. Raue said. Previous waves of technology have promised to eliminate repetitive work but have often increased workloads instead, said Ema Roloff, Madison, Wisconsin-based cofounder and chief growth officer of Roloff Consulting. “What we are seeing a lot of happening is the manual repetitive work being taken away, and instead of opening up capacity for what most people would see as the more important work, we’re shoving more work onto people’s plates,” she said. Although women may face a higher risk of job displacement, their industry knowledge, communication skills and ability to build relationships could become increasingly valuable as AI takes over routine tasks, Ms. Roloff said. Companies that focus too heavily on eliminating positions risk losing employees who understand their businesses and customers, she said. Heavy workloads also leave women little time to experiment with AI, making training important, Ms. Raue said. “If your company’s not offering you opportunities to learn in that space, go out and learn them yourself because you’re going to need them and you’re going to make yourself more valuable that way,” she said. Ms. Raue cautioned that outright resistance to AI could heighten the risk of displacement. “The more you fight it, the more they’re going to try to replace you with it,” she said. Women should also build professional relationships to help them navigate career changes and actively seek sponsors who can advocate for them and open doors to new opportunities, said Lorene Phillips, founder of Bermuda-based consultancy Clarendon Wallace. “Build your network before you need it,” she said during a separate presentation. Women should seek out senior leaders willing to use their influence to help them advance rather than waiting for sponsorship opportunities to arise, she said. “If you don’t have one, find one. Search for one, but you need one,” Ms. Phillips said. Thierry Léger, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of global reinsurance firm SCOR, explained this morning that while the market is more competitive, with a proliferation of new capital entering, he sees this as an opportunity for the company, while suggesting that if there are better ways to match risk and capital they should be exploited. items.extracted_text: SCOR sees competition from broker facilities, third-party capital as opportunity: CEO Léger - Artemis.bm SCOR sees competition from broker facilities, third-party capital as opportunity: CEO Léger - Artemis.bm SCOR sees competition from broker facilities, third-party capital as opportunity: CEO Léger 30th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Thierry Léger, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of global reinsurance firm SCOR, explained this morning that while the market is more competitive, with a proliferation of new capital entering, he sees this as an opportunity for the company, while suggesting that if there are better ways to match risk and capital they should be exploited. As our sister publication Reinsurance News reported earlier, SCOR delivered net income of €206 million in the third quarter of 2026 , driven by a strong group performance including a 3.5% rise in P&C insurance revenue to €1.9 billion and a combined ratio of 84.1%. SCOR’s results did highlight “deteriorating reinsurance margins” though, which is inevitable in a softened and highly competitive market environment. But the reinsurer’s CEO feels there are still attractive opportunities to be had, while the developments seen in the marketplace should not necessarily be viewed as negative. Commenting on the outlook for the end of year reinsurance renewals, Léger said, “Our P&C teams are now fully-focused on the 1st of January 2027 renewals. We expect competition to remain high and have a clear priority for our underwriters, margin and quality over volume. Over recent years, we have strengthened our capital discipline, remaining very selective and deploying capital only when risk-return is attractive. In the last weeks, we announced the exit of U.S. casualty and space of our direct insurance business due to lack of adequate margins and an unchanged negative outlook for these lines of business. Our tier one franchise technical expertise across P&C and life and health, and our strategic capital allocation to diversifying and profitable lines of business position us well ahead of the next strategic cycle and to navigate market headwinds.” Later during the call he was asked about how competition shows up in SCOR’s results, on which Léger acknowledged the inevitability that effects will be seen over-time. “Imagine it’s like a wave coming, and it’s coming also for us. So those results will slowly earn through IFRS 17, slowly earn through our quarterly results in the one to two years to come. We feel still limited impact from it, it’s still a bit too early, but we will see it next year, then the year after. “So there is pressure on the margins and we have been able to compensate the pressure with a bit more volume. So if you multiply volume times margins, we are still in a very good spot, and that’s really what we call portfolio steering. “We really try to steer our portfolio in the best possible way, allocate capacity, capital to the most attractive portfolios in a very dynamic way that allows us to still find attractive areas to grow. “But as I said at the beginning, we are in a more competitive environment. That’s what we are preparing for. I think that SCOR has very good cards to continue to write profitable business in the year to come.” During the call, Léger was asked for his views on broker-led reinsurance facilities in the market, which the CEO linked together with third-party capital and explained that it’s not necessarily all bad for the reinsurers. “On the broker-led reinsurance facilities, first of all we think that competition is there for a reason, right? I mean, if there are different ways, better ways to conduct business, then I think that’s what competition is here for. These things have to be exploited, these opportunitie,” Léger said. Continuing to explain that, “We see quite a dynamic and quite active broker environment, coming up with facilities that they haven’t maybe presented before. They’re using third-party capital in a way they haven’t done before, and so it’s not just the type of structures, they’re not new, but maybe the quantity of which come up right now probably a big link to the softening market. “However, for SCOR, we are always looking at those as an opportunity, what can we learn from it, what can we apply to us and how can we position SCOR in a nimble way to actually make those developments an opportunity. “So far, I would say it is much more in our camp now to react to it and understand what’s going on. I’m pretty confident that we will be able to make it an opportunity for SCOR, accepting that the environment is what it is, and we have to adapt and we have to make the best out of it.” SCOR is already utilising third-party capital within its business in numerous ways, from its retrocession purchases, to risk-sharing arrangements and of course its asset management arm SCOR Investment Partners through its insurance-linked securities (ILS) funds. During the Monte Carlo reinsurance event, Léger had said that the reinsurer sees third-party capital as an attractive source of capital for the firm, and sees no future changes regarding its strategy for managing it . Naturally, the largest reinsurance companies in the world have sufficient access to underwriting flow, as well as the data to support major investors entry into the market in support of their business, which positions players like SCOR to lean more heavily on third-party investors should they choose to. At a time when brokers are pulling significant new capital into a softening market, the reinsurers natural and best response may be to identify how these trends can be leant into, to help them make their own businesses more efficient as well. items.extracted_text: Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack: How Crypto Insurance Works Article 2 Comments Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world’s biggest crypto heist, putting a spotlight on how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks. But insurance protection is far from uniform. Coverage depends on how assets are stored, how hackers gain access and the specific terms of the policy. Limited regulation and volatile crypto prices have long made insurers wary of the sector, despite growing demand for protection against digital asset theft and claims against company executives. Read more: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto’s Biggest-Ever Heist While both crime and demand for protection have tracked cryptocurrencies’ meteoric rise, underwriting such risks remains a niche business offered largely by specialist insurers in the Lloyd’s market and in Bermuda. WHAT IS DIGITAL ASSET INSURANCE? Digital asset insurance is a range of policies designed to protect cryptocurrency exchanges, custodians and other companies operating in the sector against financial losses arising from the theft of digital assets, cyberattacks, technology failures and other business risks. Unlike traditional insurance, these policies are tailored to risks associated with blockchain technology, including the theft or loss of private keys, wallet security breaches, smart contract vulnerabilities and failures in digital asset custody. The global crypto insurance market was valued at $9.37 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $184.98 billion by 2033, according to Data Bridge Market Research. The research firm cited growing institutional adoption of cryptocurrencies and rising incidents of cyberattacks and digital asset theft among the factors driving demand. Coverage can include several types of policies: Crime insurance for theft, social engineering and scams Cyber liability for breaches, hacks and regulatory response Errors and omissions insurance for software bugs, smart contract failures Directors and officers insurance for lawsuits targeting executives Technology liability for infrastructure providers HOW ARE LOSSES COVERED? When a crypto exchange suffers a hack, losses can be covered through a combination of insurance payouts, the company’s own capital and emergency funds set aside to compensate customers. The extent of insurance coverage depends on the policies held by the exchange, including their limits, deductibles and exclusions. Where losses exceed the insured amount, the company must rely on its own financial resources or other recovery arrangements to meet its obligations. Some exchanges also maintain reserve funds to reimburse customers following security breaches. Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents. As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance’s website. The company did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment on its insurance coverage. WHAT CAN PREVENT AN INSURANCE PAYOUT? Exclusions that allow insurers to deny certain claims are common in policies covering digital assets as well as the personal liabilities of directors and officers at cryptocurrency companies. These can limit the scope of protection available to companies and make it harder for them to secure coverage. Common exclusions in these policies include value fluctuations, fraudulent acts by the policyholder and unsecured or negligent key management. “Digital asset firms and, increasingly, their institutional clients need to understand precisely what is covered, where exclusions and sublimits apply, and which risks are retained,” Jacqueline Quintal, Marsh’s financial institutions and digital asset industry leader, told Reuters. “Given the potential gap between probable/possible loss and available insurance capacity, technology and security controls, strong governance and financial strength are equally important to resilience.” DO TRADITIONAL CRIME AND CYBER INSURANCE POLICIES COVER CRYPTO? Most standard crime insurance policies do not cover cryptocurrency losses, as they were originally designed to protect physical property such as cash, securities and precious metals. Traditional cyber liability policies also do not always cover the value of digital assets stolen in a hack. While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds. As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added. HOW DO INSURERS ASSESS CRYPTO THEFT CLAIMS? Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy’s coverage. They may also assess whether the exchange followed required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals. The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss. items.extracted_text: Markel Expects to See Runoff Certainty With Enstar’s $1.2B Adverse Development Cover Article 0 Comments Markel Group has entered into a reinsurance runoff agreement with Enstar Group, the legacy acquisition specialist that is providing $1.2 billion of adverse development cover for underwriting years 2025 and prior. “[W]e are taking decisive action on legacy exposures,” said Simon Wilson, chief executive officer of Markel Insurance, during an analysts’ call to discuss the group’s third quarter results. Wilson explained that the ADC provides “greater certainty around the runoff” of its Global Reinsurance division and other exited lines such as professional liability and architects and engineers. “This is about creating greater certainty around the run-off and allowing us to focus even more squarely on the ongoing specialty insurance business,” he told the analysts. “The ADC reinsurance agreement includes subject reserves of $4.8 billion, of which Markel will retain the first $2.6 billion and retrocede the next $2.3 billion to Enstar,” according to Markel Group in a statement . “Markel will obtain adverse loss development coverage of $1.2 billion above the $4.8 billion of subject reserves under the transaction terms and pay Enstar a risk premium of $120 million,” Markel continued. The ADC was completed between Markel Insurance, the insurance operations within Markel Group, and Enstar Group’s wholly owned subsidiary, Cavello Bay Reinsurance Ltd. Markel will retain administrative and claims handling responsibilities for the portfolio. Completion of the transaction is expected by the end of the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to the receipt of regulatory approval and satisfaction of other customary closing conditions. As part of its strategy to focus on core specialty insurance markets, Markel Insurance sold the renewal rights for its $1.2 billion reinsurance business to Nationwide in August 2025 . Markel’s reinsurance division was then placed into orderly runoff. “The agreement will give Markel greater certainty over its legacy liabilities as it focuses on growing its core specialty insurance business. We look forward to continuing our work with Simon Wilson and his team once the transaction closes,” commented Dominic Silvester, Enstar’s chief executive officer, in a statement announcing the deal . During the analysts’ call, Brian Costanzo, chief financial officer of Markel Insurance, explained that the ADC transaction does not include the $205 million reserving charge for its fronting carrier subsidiary State National, which had issued paper for a now-bankrupt reinsurer. (Editor’s note: the reinsurer capacity provider is Fleming International Re, currently in managed, orderly runoff). “This marks the first substantial credit loss in State National’s over 40-year history,” said Thomas Gayner, chief executive officer of Markel Group, during the company’s Q2 analysts’ call. Regarding the advisers for the ADC transaction, Enstar said Insurance Advisory Partners LLC acted its financial adviser to Enstar, while Aon acted as reinsurance broker and adviser to Markel. items.extracted_text: Meta Settles With Teen During Trial Testing Claims Social Media Caused Depression, Eating Disorders Article 0 Comments Meta Platforms has settled with a teen plaintiff who accused the company of designing Instagram and Facebook to be addictive, causing her mental health problems and disordered eating, attorneys for the plaintiff said on Friday. The settlement came after jury selection began on Wednesday for a trial that was slated to test the claims of two teens, identified as S.J. and K.D.B., against Meta and Snapchat parent Snap Inc. Meta had settled with S.J. days before the trial, so Friday’s settlement with K.D.B. means the trial is expected to proceed against Snap only. Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply “We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client,” Emily Jeffcott, an attorney for K.D.B., said in a statement. The trial is the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media after Meta, Snap, TikTok and Alphabet’s YouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use. S.J. and K.D.B. had previously settled with TikTok and YouTube. The case was selected among the thousands of pending lawsuits as a test case, so the jury’s verdict could influence how the companies and plaintiffs resolve similar cases. S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age 9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll. The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make the apps safe places for young people to express themselves. Social media companies face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide. In the first case to go to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube had been negligent and awarded a young woman $6 million in damages. The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the companies. The first school district chosen for trial settled with all of the companies. In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every state and U.S. territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over the platforms’ harm to teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens. Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion penalty after a jury found the company misled Facebook users about the privacy of their data and how it handles hate speech. The company has said it will appeal. (Reporting by Jones Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Matthew Lewis) Copyright 2026 Reuters. Click for restrictions . Was this article valuable?
